opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's one of the more underappreciated asymmetries in this field. When you're improving the driving itself, there's a fairly well-understood recipe now: you collect more diverse data, you scale up the models, you invest in compute, and you generally see steady gains. The model gets smoother, more humanlike, it handles more situations gracefully. Those scaling trends are real and we lean into them.

But testing is a different problem. To deploy, you don't just need to show the system is good on average. You need confidence that it's safe in the long tail, in the rare, high-stakes events that might happen once in millions of miles. And as the system gets better, those failures become rarer, which means you need disproportionately more evidence to say anything statistically meaningful about them. So the better your driver gets, the harder validating it becomes. Improvement and evaluation pull in opposite directions in terms of cost.

You also can't just replay logged data, because the moment your planner does something different from what the human or the previous system did, the other agents should react differently. Open-loop evaluation breaks down. So you need closed-loop simulation with realistic, reactive agents, and realistic sensor simulation if you're testing end-to-end. Building that is its own research problem, arguably as hard as driving, because now you need models of everyone else on the road that are realistic, diverse, and controllable, including adversarially, so you can surface the hard cases intentionally rather than waiting to stumble on them.

And then there's the question of what "good" means. You need metrics and evaluators that capture safety, comfort, and road etiquette in ways that correlate with real-world outcomes, and that generalize when you change the model architecture. Every time you change the stack, you want to know quickly whether you've regressed somewhere subtle.

So my view is that the field's progress on driving quality has somewhat outpaced the progress on validation. Scaling the driver is something many teams can now do. Scaling the ability to prove it's safe enough to remove the human, across new cities, new conditions, new vehicle platforms, that's where a lot of the real work, and frankly a lot of the competitive advantage, lies.

r001.rationale: It contrasts improving driving through more data and compute with testing, where rarer failures require disproportionately more evidence.

r002.rationale: It says hard cases should be surfaced intentionally, but does not state that experts must anticipate potential failure modes.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we think about a lot at Waymo, and I think it's an important distinction. When you're improving the driver, scaling is in some sense the easy story. You collect more data, you build bigger models, you train on more diverse situations, and the model gets better at the common cases and, increasingly, at the rare ones. That's the standard machine learning story, and it works. It's a very satisfying loop.

Testing is a different problem, and I'd argue a harder one, because what you care about in testing is not the average case. You care about the tail. You're trying to answer the question: is this driver safe across the full distribution of things that can happen on the road, including things that happen once every million miles, or once every ten million miles? And the issue is that no matter how much data you collect, the events that matter most for safety are, almost by definition, the ones you have the fewest examples of. So you can't just drive more miles and hope you've covered it. The miles you'd need to drive to see enough of these rare events, with statistical confidence, is enormous. Billions of miles. And you'd have to redo it every time you change the model.

So testing has to scale along a different axis. Instead of scaling the amount of real-world experience, you have to scale your ability to generate and evaluate situations that you may never have seen, or seen only once. That's where simulation becomes central. You take the logs you have, and you perturb them. You change the behavior of other agents. You make the pedestrian step out a half second earlier, you make the car ahead brake harder, you add an occlusion. You construct scenarios synthetically from a structured understanding of what the risky situations look like. And then you need realistic agents in that simulation, because if the other road users don't react believably to what your vehicle does, the test tells you very little. So ironically, a lot of the same modeling machinery we use for driving, we end up turning around and using to build the test environment.

The other thing that's different is the question of coverage. With driving, you can measure progress with a metric and watch it go up. With testing, you have to ask whether your test suite is actually representative of the risk you'll encounter. That requires a lot of structure: taxonomies of scenarios, an understanding of what a competent human driver would do, metrics that capture not just collision or no collision but the quality of the behavior. And you need to reason about how a change in one part of the system propagates to outcomes, because you're evaluating a closed-loop system, not a classifier.

So I'd put it this way. Improving the driver scales with data and compute in a fairly direct way. Testing scales with your ability to model the world well enough to ask it counterfactual questions, and that's a fundamentally more open-ended research problem. In some ways I find it the more interesting one.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts improving the driver through more data and compute with testing, which cannot scale by simply driving more miles because rare safety events need enormous mileage to observe.

r002.rationale: The response discusses constructing risky scenarios and organizing test coverage, but does not state that experts must anticipate potential failure modes.

astra-6.text:
I think the distinction is that improving the model and demonstrating that it’s safe are two different problems. As you collect more data, you can use it to improve the model’s ability to perceive the world, predict what other road users will do, and make driving decisions. You can get better at many situations through that process.

But testing is asking, “What are we still getting wrong, and how often does that happen?” As the system gets better, those failures become rarer. So you need increasingly more driving to observe enough failures to understand whether a change actually improved safety. And aggregate mileage alone doesn’t tell you whether you’ve covered the situations that matter.

That’s why you need more targeted testing, including simulation and challenging scenarios. More training data helps you improve the driver, but validating that improvement requires coverage of rare events and a way to measure progress reliably.

r001.rationale: It contrasts improvement through more data with validation, explaining that rarer failures require increasingly more driving and targeted coverage to assess safety.

r002.rationale: It mentions finding failures and testing challenging or rare scenarios, but does not state that experts must anticipate potential failure modes.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, when you’re improving the driver, you can collect more data, train on it, and measure whether performance gets better. Testing has a different challenge: you’re trying to establish that the system behaves safely, including in situations that are extremely rare. Simply adding more ordinary driving miles doesn’t necessarily give you much more evidence about those situations.

And as the driver gets better, the failures become rarer, so you need increasingly more exposure to find them. That’s why simulation and targeted testing are so important. You want to take a challenging interaction, vary the conditions, and understand where the system succeeds or fails. More data helps both, but testing needs coverage of the situations that matter, not just volume.

r001.rationale: It contrasts improvement through collecting more data with testing for rare situations, explaining that ordinary miles may add little evidence and that testing needs relevant coverage, not just volume.

r002.rationale: It mentions targeted testing of challenging interactions but does not state that experts must anticipate potential failure modes.
